articleHeadline: Giardia, the Hidden Passenger in Our Small Intestine.
articleSummary: Giardia duodenalis (G. lamblia/intestinalis) is a flagellated protozoan with two forms—trophozoite in the small intestine and cysts shed in stool that spread infection. Transmission is fecal-oral via contaminated water or food; cysts resist usual chlorination, making boiling water a reliable disinfection. Globally, giardiasis affects about 400 million people. Symptoms vary from acute or chronic diarrhea and malnutrition to asymptomatic carriage, more common among children in developing countries. Diagnosis is challenging because cysts/trophozoites are intermittently shed; typical approaches include stool microscopy (often repeated), antigen tests (ELISA/EIA) with higher sensitivity, and PCR (high accuracy but costly). In Bandung, Indonesia, 12.1% of 99 stunted children carried intestinal parasites, Giardia accounting for ~9%. National stunting was 27.6% in 2019; West Java 31.06%. Treatments are nitroimidazoles (metronidazole; tinidazole, secnidazole, nitazoxanid) with possible resistance. Prevention focuses on boiled water, hygienic food handling, and handwashing.
